texts: mixed: the burning, its lantern and the wintergloss it burns are right, but "alongside mire-essence" survives only as an opaque preposition record — nothing says the mire-essence burns too, so a later question about what the lantern burns will not find it. If both substances burn, write "A lantern burns wintergloss and mire-essence.", which gives each substance its own burning. If you meant the mire-essence merely sits beside the burning, say that instead: "A lantern burns wintergloss next to a pot of mire-essence."

mixed: "that lantern" resolves correctly to the lantern of the first sentence and every part of the question is well formed, but "what happens to" leaves the verb unnamed, so the moths get pinned into one single role and the question will miss any event that filed them under a different one; "at that lantern" is likewise recorded as where the moths stand rather than where the happening is. Ask it from the actor's side — "What do the nightmoths at that lantern do?" — or name the event you are really asking about, e.g. "Does that lantern's burning draw the nightmoths?"; either one fixes the moths' role.
